p: The debrief was Thursday at four in the briefing room, two days after the shirt tail went up on the corkboard, and Abby had already written it on the whiteboard in green before Jordan got there. SOLO 10/20. WHAT WENT RIGHT. WHAT YOU'D WANT BACK. WHAT'S NEXT.

They did the first two columns in forty minutes. The door. The float on the second approach. The go-around, which Abby circled. Jordan had come straight from sleeping off a shift that had ended at seven, and she kept her coffee in both hands and answered everything in order, the way she'd give a report at the ER doors. Abby wrote it all down and didn't say good once, which Jordan had learned meant it was.
Under WHAT'S NEXT there were three lines. 1. Solo laps until I'm bored. 2. Hood work and the practice area. 3. You.

Abby slid a stapled packet across the table. The cover said RISK MANAGEMENT HANDBOOK, CHAPTER 2, PERSONAL MINIMUMS, and under that, in Abby's capitals, FILL IN EVERY BOX. NOT MY NUMBERS. YOURS. Next chapter in the book is the pilot. It's the part of the airplane that fails the most, and it doesn't have a squawk list. I don't sign you for the practice area alone until that's done.
Jordan put it in her flight bag, next to the green notebook. It stayed there for two weeks.

Afterward she went out to the ramp and sat in Biscuit for a minute with the door open, the way she'd started doing, not for any reason. The low sun came in across the panel. Above the mag switch, above Ellie's HI DAD sticker with its corners curling, there was a rectangle of paint a shade darker than the rest of the panel, a little bigger than a playing card, with two old corners of yellowed tape still stuck to it. She'd seen it in April and filed it the way you file a scar on a patient: something used to be there. She looked at it longer this time. She still didn't ask anybody.
At 8:14 that night her mother texted.
A text from Lourdes Reyes. Thursday the 5th is your brother's birthday. Pozole at mine at 12. Bring back my good bowls. Claire will come after work.

She'd traded that shift away in September, the first trade she'd made all year, and hadn't told anybody why. She put the lunch in her phone. Then she sat looking at the date for a while. He'd have been forty two.
The club chat, meanwhile, had found the weather.

A message from Marisol Tran. First cold week coming. Biscuit's cabin heat is a shroud around the muffler. If you pull the knob all the way out, open a vent too. Look at the CO card by the compass when you do. I mean it.
A message from Russ Kim. marisol is the only person alive who can make heat sound threatening
Abby's Ground School: the part of the airplane that's you.

Sit. We've spent six months on the airplane: the engine, the weather, the air, the box around the runway. Today is the part that fails most often, and it's the one sitting in your chair. The handbook calls it human factors and doesn't soften it. Most accidents trace back to a decision somebody made. Usually a reasonable sounding one, made a little tired, a little late, by a person who wanted the flight to happen.

The FAA's name for doing this on purpose is aeronautical decision making, ADM. The PHAK makes a claim I like: good judgment can be taught. The old idea was that judgment grows by itself as you log hours. It doesn't, or not reliably. ADM is a set of habits. Spot the attitudes that hurt pilots. Learn to change the behavior. Learn to recognize stress and cope with it. Build risk assessment skills. Use every resource you've got. Then grade yourself afterward on how you decided, and not only on how it turned out.

Two words the test treats carefully. A hazard is the thing itself: a condition, an event, a circumstance. A nick in the prop. Gusts on the ATIS. Four hours of sleep. Risk is your assessment of what that hazard could do to you, how likely and how bad. Two pilots can look at the same hazard and see different risk, which is why this chapter exists.

Risk management has four principles, and I want them in this order. Accept no unnecessary risk. Make risk decisions at the appropriate level, which means the pilot in command, and the handbook says never let anyone else make them for you, not ATC and not your passengers. Accept risk when the benefits outweigh the costs. And build risk management into planning at every level, in the air too, not only at the kitchen table.

Over all of it the handbook puts single-pilot resource management, SRM: the art and science of managing all the resources available to a single pilot, on board and outside, before and during the flight. It bundles ADM, risk management, task management, automation management, CFIT awareness (controlled flight into terrain, which is flying a perfectly good airplane into the ground), and situational awareness. Alone, there's nobody in the right seat to catch you. SRM is what you use instead. ATC is a resource. A passenger who's never flown is a resource; they can look for traffic. Your checklist is a resource. So is calling it off.
How the exam asks it. Know hazard versus risk, the four risk management principles, and the pieces of SRM. "Never let ATC or passengers make risk decisions for you" is straight from the handbook.

Since the discovery flight I've asked you the same thing at the wing. Sleep, meds, sick, anything. That's IMSAFE with the letters filed off. The AIM calls it a personal checklist and says to run it on yourself the way you run one on the airplane, because pilot impairment contributes to many more accidents than failures of aircraft systems.

Illness: am I sick? The AIM's safest rule is not to fly with any illness. A cold you'd work through on the ambulance is a cold that blocks your ears on the way down. Medication: am I taking anything that might affect my judgment or make me drowsy? Stress: pressure from the job, money, health, family. The handbook points out that the regulations list conditions that ground you and stress isn't one, so nobody's going to count it for you. Alcohol: have I been drinking within 8 hours? Within 24? Fatigue: am I tired and not adequately rested? Emotion: am I emotionally upset?

The AIM's paragraph on emotion is short. I'll read it once and then leave it alone. Certain emotionally upsetting events, including a serious argument, death of a family member, separation or divorce, loss of job, and financial catastrophe, can render a pilot unable to fly an aircraft safely. Any pilot who experiences an emotionally upsetting event should not fly until satisfactorily recovered from it. The PHAK lists a death in the family by name under psychological stress. So grief is on the checklist. It sits there the way icing sits in a weather briefing: real, and hard to see from the inside, and able to change what a day can hold.

There's a regulation behind part of this. 61.53 says a person who holds a medical certificate may not act as pilot in command while they know or have reason to know of any medical condition that would make them unable to meet the requirements for that medical, or while they're taking medication or getting other treatment for a condition that leaves them unable to meet those requirements. Your medical says you were fit the day the doctor saw you. 61.53 makes you the one who checks it again on the day you fly.

The handbook gets specific about pills. Over the counter antihistamines and decongestants can cause drowsiness and fuzzy thinking. Diphenhydramine, Benadryl, gets called out by name, because it makes you drowsy and stays in your system a long time. The AIM's safest rule is not to fly while taking any medication unless the FAA has approved it. And remember that the condition you're treating can ground you by itself. The pill makes you feel better. It doesn't make the cold go away.
How the exam asks it. Expect IMSAFE letter by letter, 61.53's two prohibitions, and the point that stress isn't a regulatory grounding condition but still has to be counted.

91.17 is four lines and the test loves all of them. No person may act or attempt to act as a crewmember of a civil aircraft within 8 hours after the consumption of any alcoholic beverage, while under the influence of alcohol, while using any drug that affects the person's faculties in any way contrary to safety, or while having an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater in a blood or breath specimen. Those are four separate rules. Ten hours after your last beer with a 0.05, you're grounded. Seven hours after one beer with a 0.00, you're grounded. And the PHAK says it in plain words: while experiencing a hangover, a pilot is still under the influence of alcohol.

The same section says you can't let a person who appears intoxicated ride in your airplane, except in an emergency or a medical patient under proper care, which you know what looks like better than I do. If an authorized law enforcement officer asks you to take a test, you take it. And the FAA can ask for the results of any test taken within 4 hours after you flew.

Now the numbers that aren't regulations. A 12 ounce light beer, a 4 ounce glass of table wine, and a shot of liquor all carry about half an ounce of alcohol. The handbook says your body needs about 3 hours to get rid of one drink, and that considerable amounts can stay in you for over 16 hours. The AIM calls 8 hours the legal line and then says an excellent rule is 12 to 24 hours between bottle and throttle, depending on how much. Altitude makes it worse. Alcohol keeps the brain from using oxygen, a kind of histotoxic hypoxia, and the PHAK says one ounce of alcohol can equal about 2,000 extra feet of physiological altitude. You live at 5,885 feet. Do that math before the second beer.

Drugs. The FAA's position on marijuana is in the handbook in quotes: marijuana is an illicit drug per federal law and its use by airmen is prohibited. The dispensary down the road doesn't change that. You hold a federal certificate. Stimulants count too: caffeine, nicotine, the energy drink at hour twenty of a shift. They're drugs, and their main trick is hiding fatigue from you.
How the exam asks it. The four parts of 91.17 are separate tests and you have to pass all four. 8 hours and 0.04 are the numbers. The AIM's 12 to 24 hours is a recommendation, not the rule.

Fatigue goes at the top of your list, because of your job. The handbook says fatigue is frequently associated with pilot error, and the AIM says it may not be apparent to a pilot until serious errors are made. You have a long history of being good at things while exhausted. Alone in a cockpit, that history is a hazard.

Two kinds. Acute fatigue is short term: a long day, hard work, excitement, a night without sleep. The AIM's list of causes includes heavy mental workload and strong emotional pressure, which I'd like you to notice. Rest and 8 hours of sound sleep usually fix it. A special kind is skill fatigue. Your timing goes a little off, so a landing turns into separate pieces instead of one motion, and your attention shrinks to the middle of your vision. That's when the airspeed you aren't looking at wanders off. Chronic fatigue is when there's not enough recovery between the acute ones, over weeks or months. It usually has psychological roots, rest alone doesn't cure it, and the handbook says see a physician.

The rule is one sentence. If you're suffering from acute fatigue, stay on the ground. The handbook says no amount of training or experience overcomes it once it's in the flight deck with you, and it says to avoid flying without a full night's rest, after working excessive hours, or after an especially exhausting or stressful day. You've made that call once already, in a parking lot at 7:25 in the morning. Make it every time.

Dehydration sits right next to it. Denver is dry, Biscuit's cabin heat is drier, and coffee is a diuretic. The first noticeable effect of dehydration, the handbook says, is fatigue. It suggests two to four quarts of water every 24 hours, and points out that thirst shows up late, around a quart and a half down or 2 percent of your body weight. Carry a bottle. Drink before you want it. And eat. Missed meals and low blood sugar are on the handbook's list of physiological stressors, and a granola bar standing up in the station kitchen is a snack, at best.

The ACS also lists hypothermia, which out here means dressing for where you might land instead of where you took off. A wheat field east of Bennett in November is a cold place to wait for somebody to find you. The PAVE checklist asks whether you have the clothing, water, and survival gear for the route. In a Cessna with a heater that works some of the time, the answer is a real coat.
How the exam asks it. "If suffering from acute fatigue, stay on the ground." Know acute versus chronic, and that fatigue is often invisible to the tired pilot.

Hypoxia means not enough oxygen, and the brain is the first organ that minds. The handbook sorts it four ways by cause. Hypoxic hypoxia is not enough getting in. At altitude the air is still about 21 percent oxygen, but the pressure is lower, so fewer molecules make it across in your lungs. Hypemic hypoxia is blood that can't carry what's there: anemia, bleeding, a recent blood donation, and most often carbon monoxide parked on your hemoglobin. Stagnant hypoxia is blood that isn't moving: shock, a heart not pumping well, high G loads, cold. Histotoxic hypoxia is cells that can't use the oxygen they're given: alcohol, narcotics, poisons.

The first symptoms can be euphoria and a carefree feeling, which is the meanest line in the book. You feel great right up to the part where you can't add. Then headache, slower reactions, impaired judgment, visual impairment, drowsiness, dizziness, tingling, numbness, and cyanosis, blue lips and fingernails. Your field of vision narrows. The AIM says a normal healthy pilot usually doesn't see significant effects below 12,000 feet, that from 12,000 to 15,000 judgment, memory, alertness, and coordination go, and that performance can seriously deteriorate within 15 minutes at 15,000. One detail for us: night vision starts to deteriorate at a cabin altitude as low as 5,000 feet. Centennial is 5,885. Every night flight you ever take here starts above that line.

Time of useful consciousness is how long you have to make rational, lifesaving decisions and carry them out at a given altitude without supplemental oxygen. The handbook's table: 30 minutes or more at 20,000 feet, 5 to 10 minutes at 22,000, 3 to 5 at 25,000, 1 to 2 at 30,000, and 9 to 15 seconds at 45,000. Biscuit will never see 20,000. Look at the shape of the curve. It falls off a cliff.

Then the regulation, 91.211. At cabin pressure altitudes above 12,500 feet MSL up to and including 14,000, the required minimum flight crew has to be provided with and use supplemental oxygen for the part of the flight at those altitudes that's more than 30 minutes long. Above 14,000, the crew uses it the entire time. Above 15,000, each occupant has to be provided with supplemental oxygen. Provided. The passengers don't have to wear it. The test likes that word. In an unpressurized airplane, cabin altitude is the altitude you're flying.

The AIM goes further than the rule and recommends oxygen above 10,000 feet in the day and above 5,000 at night. Living in Denver doesn't buy you anything. The handbook says all pilots are susceptible, regardless of physical endurance or acclimatization. Treatment is lower altitude, supplemental oxygen, or both.
How the exam asks it. Match the hypoxia type to its cause (CO is hypemic, alcohol is histotoxic). Know the three altitude bands in 91.211 and the word "provided" above 15,000.

Hyperventilation is the opposite problem: breathing too fast and too deep, so you blow off too much carbon dioxide. It happens more than people think, usually when something scares you. Symptoms overlap with hypoxia: lightheaded, dizzy, tingling, hot and cold, muscle spasms, visual impairment, and at the end, unconsciousness. The fix is to slow your breathing on purpose. The handbook says talking out loud helps, and a paper bag works. You talk to yourself in the pattern. I've noticed. Keep doing it. If you're ever on oxygen when symptoms start, the AIM says go to 100 percent oxygen and check the system first, because the two can happen at the same time.

Ears. Your middle ear connects to your throat through the Eustachian tube. Going up, the air inside expands and leaks out on its own. Coming down, the outside pressure rises and you have to open the tube yourself: swallow, yawn, or close your mouth, pinch your nose, and blow gently, the Valsalva maneuver. With a cold the tube may not open at all. That's an ear block: severe pain, hearing loss for hours or days, sometimes a ruptured eardrum. A sinus block is the same thing in your sinuses, worst on descent, sometimes bad enough to make your upper teeth ache. The AIM's prevention is the same for both: don't fly with an upper respiratory infection or a nasal allergy. It also says decongestant sprays and drops usually aren't adequate protection, and that oral decongestants have side effects that can impair you. So the cure for a stuffy nose is a day off.

Motion sickness is your brain getting messages from your eyes and your inner ear that don't agree. Plenty of students get it in the first few lessons and it fades. Anxiety makes it worse. Open the fresh air vents, look outside at the horizon, keep your head still, and tell me. It's no reflection on you as a pilot. Dramamine helps passengers. The handbook doesn't recommend it for pilots, because it makes you drowsy.

One more the ACS lists: nitrogen after scuba diving. The AIM wants at least 12 hours before flying up to 8,000 feet after diving that didn't need decompression stops, and at least 24 hours after diving that did. Above 8,000 feet, at least 24 hours after any dive. The nitrogen you soaked up at depth comes out of solution when the pressure drops, and it comes out in your joints.
How the exam asks it. Hyperventilation looks like hypoxia, and the fix is to slow down your breathing. Ear and sinus blocks are worst on descent.

Biscuit's cabin heat is outside air run through a metal shroud wrapped around the exhaust muffler. It's simple and it works, and if the muffler cracks, your heat comes with exhaust in it. The AIM says heaters like that, with exhaust escaping through cracks and seals, cause several nonfatal and fatal accidents every year.

CO is colorless, odorless, and tasteless. It grabs hemoglobin about 200 times more easily than oxygen does, which is hypemic hypoxia, and the body can take up to 48 hours to clear it. If you smell exhaust, assume CO is there. If you smell nothing, that tells you nothing. Symptoms: headache, blurred vision, dizziness, drowsiness, loss of muscle power. Biscuit has a disposable detector card on the panel by the compass, and it darkens when there's CO around. Look at it the way you look at the oil pressure.

What you do: shut off the heater, open the fresh air vents and the window, use oxygen if you have it, and get on the ground. The AIM adds that if the symptoms are severe or don't go away after landing, get medical treatment. Then tell Marisol, because whatever made the CO is still in the airplane waiting for Russ. And smokers start the day behind. The handbook says smoking at sea level can put enough CO in your blood to feel like flying at 8,000 feet.
How the exam asks it. Suspect CO with a headache, drowsiness, or dizziness while the heater's on. The first actions are heater off and fresh air.

Three systems tell you which way is up. Your eyes. Your vestibular system, the fluid-filled semicircular canals and otolith organs in your inner ears. And your somatosensory system, the nerves in your skin, muscles, and joints, which is where seat of the pants flying lives. On a clear day your eyes win every argument. Lose the horizon, in a cloud, on a moonless night over the plains, and the other two get loud. They lie, and they sound sure.

The canals have a blind spot. Anything slower than about 2 degrees per second of rotation, they miss. And hold a turn long enough and the fluid catches up with the canal walls, so the turn stops registering at all. Most of the list comes out of that one fact. The leans: you've rolled slowly into a bank you never felt, you level the wings, and now you feel banked the other way, so you lean, or roll right back into the bank. Coriolis: long steady turn, you drop your head to grab the pencil off the floor, the fluid gets going on a new axis, and suddenly you're tumbling sideways through a sky that hasn't moved. The AIM says it's the most overwhelming of all illusions in flight. I believe them. Graveyard spiral: you're in a coordinated turn you can't feel, you see the altimeter unwinding, it feels like a wings-level descent, so you pull back. Pull in a bank and what you mostly get is more turn. Down it winds. Graveyard spin: same trick, played on you right after a spin recovery.

Then the otoliths, which sense straight-line acceleration and honestly can't tell it from tilt. Somatogravic illusion: shove the throttle in on takeoff and it feels like the nose is coming up, so the confused pilot pushes over toward the dirt. Yank the power back and it's reversed; they pull toward a stall. Inversion illusion: go abruptly from climb to level and it can feel like you're tumbling over backward, so they shove the nose down. Elevator illusion: an updraft feels like a climb, so they push. A downdraft feels like a dive, so they pull.

Your eyes have two of their own. A false horizon is a sloping cloud deck, or ground lights and stars smeared together at night, and you level the wings with the wrong thing. Autokinesis: stare at one light in the dark long enough and it starts to wander. Keep your eyes moving.

The cure is boring. Trust the instruments and ignore the feeling. The Airplane Flying Handbook's advice for a pilot without an instrument rating who ends up in cloud: the only concern at first is keeping the wings level, fly the attitude indicator with your fingertips, make small smooth changes, and use no more than 10 degrees of bank. And trying to fly half on the panel and half out the window, it says, is how people lose control. If you find yourself nose low with the airspeed climbing, the Instrument Flying Handbook gives the order: reduce power, level the wings with coordinated aileron and rudder, then raise the nose with smooth back pressure. Wings before pitch, same as a steep turn, for the same reason. It warns that the instinctive reaction to a nose-down attitude is to pull. That's the instinct you're training out of yourself.

Prevention beats all of it. Stay out of weather you can't see through until you're trained for it. And the handbook's list of things that make you more susceptible to disorientation reads like IMSAFE: illness, medication, alcohol, fatigue, sleep loss, mild hypoxia. The demonstration we'll do one Wednesday soon is one the handbook describes, flown with me in the airplane, gently, as high as the shelf lets us. You'll hate it. That's the point.
How the exam asks it. Match the illusion to the motion that causes it. For any disorientation question, the answer is to rely on the flight instruments.

Some illusions don't spin you. They lie about the runway. A narrower than usual runway makes you feel higher than you are, so you fly a low approach and land short. A wider one makes you feel low, so you level out high and land hard or long. An upsloping runway or upsloping terrain makes you feel high, so you go low. Downslope does the opposite. Featureless terrain, water or snow or a dark field, makes you feel high, so you go low. Pilots call that a black hole approach.

Rain on the windshield makes you feel higher than you are. Haze makes the runway look farther away, so you end up low. And here's ours: extremely clear air at a high airport can make the runway look closer than it is, so you end up high and overshoot. Fog can feel like pitching up, so pilots steepen the approach, sometimes abruptly. Bright runway lights with nothing around them look closer, so you fly high. Lights along a straight road can look like a runway.

There's a pattern. Anything that makes you feel high makes you fly low, and low is the one that hits things. The fixes are dull and they work. Expect illusions at unfamiliar airports, especially at night. Read the Chart Supplement for runway slope and lighting. Look at your altimeter on every approach, day or night. Use the PAPI when there's one. Keep your landings sharp.
How the exam asks it. Classic question: a narrower than usual runway creates the illusion of being higher than you are, leading to a lower than normal approach.
Five attitudes and the words that fix them.

The handbook names five attitudes that wreck decisions and gives each one an antidote. Memorize the antidotes word for word. That isn't me being fussy. The method is that when the thought shows up, you label it hazardous, then say the antidote, and that only works if the words come without effort.

Anti-authority: "Don't tell me." Rules, regulations, and procedures feel silly, and being told what to do makes you want to do the other thing. Antidote: Follow the rules. They are usually right. The handbook also says it's always your prerogative to question authority if you think it's in error. Question it. Then follow it while you do.
Impulsivity: "Do it quickly." Do something, anything, now, the first thing that comes to mind. Antidote: Not so fast. Think first.
Invulnerability: "It won't happen to me." You know accidents happen. You just don't feel like one is coming for you, so you take chances. Antidote: It could happen to me.
Macho: "I can do it." Trying to prove you're better than somebody, taking risks to impress. The handbook goes out of its way to say women are equally susceptible. Antidote: Taking chances is foolish.

Resignation: "What's the use?" You don't think you can change what happens, so you leave the action to others, or you go along with something unreasonable to be a nice guy. Antidote: I'm not helpless. I can make a difference.

You're going to want to tell me you don't have any of these. Everybody does, under the right pressure. You find yours by watching which one shows up when you're tired. Mine's macho, if you were wondering, and I'm aware of how that sounds from a flight instructor who tells you her hours every day.
How the exam asks it. The test gives you a thought or a situation and asks for the attitude, or gives the attitude and asks for the antidote. The wording matters.

These are the tools for doing it on purpose. PAVE is how you look for hazards before a flight: Pilot in command, Aircraft, enVironment, External pressures. Pilot is IMSAFE plus experience and currency. Aircraft is whether this airplane can do this trip: equipment, performance, fuel with reserves, the runway at the other end. Environment is weather, terrain, airports, airspace, and night. External pressures are everything outside the flight that wants it to happen: somebody waiting at the other end, a passenger you don't want to let down, wanting to show off, get-there-itis, pride. The handbook calls managing external pressure the single most important key to risk management, because it's the one category that can make you ignore the other three. Its fixes are all about leaving yourself a way out. Leave time for an extra stop. Have a backup plan. Tell the people waiting that you might be late. Carry a toothbrush.

3P is how you keep doing it once you're moving. Perceive the circumstances. Process them, by evaluating their effect on the safety of the flight. Perform, by doing the best thing. Then evaluate and go around the loop again. The handbook pairs it with two more lists. Process with CARE: consequences, alternatives, reality, external factors. Perform with TEAM: transfer, eliminate, accept, or mitigate. Transfer means handing the risk decision to someone better placed to make it, like your instructor. And the best sentence in the chapter is in the processing step: if you find yourself saying that it will probably be okay, it's definitely time for a solid reality check.

DECIDE is the other loop the test asks about: Detect that something changed, Estimate the need to react, Choose a course of action, Identify solutions, Do the necessary actions, Evaluate the effects. Then the handbook keeps a list of operational pitfalls, the traps that catch pilots with experience. Peer pressure. Mindset. Get-there-itis. Scud running. Continuing VFR into instrument conditions. Getting behind the aircraft. Losing situational awareness. Flying without adequate fuel reserves. Flying outside the envelope. Skipping the checklist because you've done it a thousand times.

Two biases the ACS names. Expectation bias is when you perceive what you expected instead of what's there. The Risk Management Handbook says it happens a lot on the ground, when a pilot who always gets the same taxi route hears the usual clearance instead of the one ATC gave. Confirmation bias is its cousin: information shows up that doesn't fit your plan, and you set it aside instead of letting it make you say uh-oh. The handbook adds that fatigue makes both worse, because a tired pilot stops taking the extra step to check.
How the exam asks it. Know what each PAVE letter covers, the 3P steps, and DECIDE. Get-there-itis is a pitfall, and external pressure is the PAVE category that feeds it.

Last thing. The regulations are the floor. They don't promise you safety, and on a bad day they'll let you do things you'd never choose on a good one. Personal minimums are limits you set for yourself, tighter than the rules, based on your own experience and proficiency. The PHAK calls it the difference between what's legal and what's smart.

The Risk Management Handbook gives six steps. Review the weather categories: VFR is ceiling greater than 3,000 feet AGL and visibility greater than 5 miles, MVFR is 1,000 to 3,000 or 3 to 5 miles, IFR and LIFR below that. Assess your experience and comfort level from your logbook, honestly. Consider the other conditions: wind, gusts, crosswind, turbulence, shortest runway, highest terrain, highest density altitude. Assemble it into a baseline. Adjust the baseline for specific conditions. Stick to the plan.

The adjustment table is where eyes glaze, so look at it. If you're facing a pilot factor like illness, medication, stress, or fatigue, or an unfamiliar airplane, or an unfamiliar airport, or a must-get-there deadline, the handbook's starting points are to add at least 500 feet to your ceiling, at least half a mile to your visibility, at least 500 feet to the runway you need, and to take at least 5 knots off the winds you'll accept. If more than one applies, it says you can adjust for each one.

Then three cautions, and the first one is the reason the card exists. Don't adjust your personal minimums to complete a specific flight. The time to change them is when you have time and can be honest, not in the parking lot with somebody waiting. Change one variable at a time. Talk to an instructor before any big change. And write them down. The handbook says a written set makes it easier to explain a tough decision to passengers who are counting on you. It makes it easier to explain to yourself, too.
Your homework is still in your bag. I can see the corner of it from here.
How the exam asks it. Personal minimums are set ahead of time and tightened, never loosened under pressure. VFR is a ceiling above 3,000 ft and visibility above 5 miles.

Friday, October 23, 5:40 in the morning. Jordan woke with her head full of wet cement and her right ear crackling every time she swallowed. Her throat felt like she'd eaten a sandbox. It was the cold that had been going around her station for two weeks, the one the captain's kid brought home from kindergarten, and she'd been sure for three shifts running that she'd dodged it.
Solo at 8. Her second one ever. Three laps in the pattern, the ones Abby wanted until she was bored. The sky out the window was clean and pink over the plains, not a breath of wind.

The bathroom cabinet had the usual: a box of diphenhydramine, a nasal spray, and a blister pack of pseudoephedrine from last winter with two tablets left. She stood holding the cabinet door open and did what she did on a scene, which was say out loud what she had. Congestion. Right ear won't clear. No fever.
A. Take the diphenhydramine, which dries her up fast, and fly at 8. It's three laps, nothing high.
B. Take the pseudoephedrine. It's the non-drowsy one, so it clears her head without slowing her.
C. Text Abby she's sick and cancel. A cold and a blocked ear mean she stays home.
D. Use the nasal spray to open up her ears, then fly. Pattern altitude is only a thousand feet up.

She types it before she's out of the bathroom. Sick. Head cold, right ear won't clear. Canceling 8am. Abby, in under a minute: ok. feel better. Then: what were you going to take. Jordan looks at the cabinet. Nothing now. good answer. that's the AIM's safest rule in one text. She makes tea, goes back to bed, and sleeps until noon. Russ takes the slot and sends a picture of pancakes from the airport diner.

That's it. The AIM's safest rule is not to fly with any illness, and congestion can cause an ear or sinus block on descent. Masking symptoms with medication adds side effects without removing the illness. Canceling costs a morning.
Decision two. The card by the compass.

Thursday, October 29, the first real cold of the year: minus three on the ramp, frost feathered on Biscuit's wings that Jordan wiped off with a towel and then checked by hand, every inch, because Abby had made her promise. Runup on Alpha near the end of 35R, mags, carb heat, both latches. She told ground she was ready for departure and ground told her to monitor tower. On the climbout she pulled the cabin heat knob all the way out, and warm air came up around her ankles smelling like hot metal and dust, which Marisol had said was normal for the first cold week.

Second lap. Downwind, 6,900. Somewhere around the turn to base she noticed a headache had moved in behind her eyes, the dull kind, and that she'd yawned twice. She'd slept eight hours. On final she looked at the little CO detector card stuck to the panel next to the compass. It was supposed to be pale. The dot in the middle had gone the gray of an old nickel.
Under her feet the heater kept blowing.
A. Leave the heat on, since it's minus three, and crack one vent a little until the headache eases.
B. Shut the heater off and finish the last lap as planned, since it should clear with the heat off.
C. Heat off, fresh air vents and the window open, then a full stop landing and tell Marisol.
D. Ignore the card. Cheap detector cards go gray with age, and she's tired from the early start.

Knob in. Both vents open, the little storm window on her door cracked, and minus three comes in like a slap, which is the point. She keeps flying the final. Centennial Tower, Niner One Echo, request full stop, possible exhaust in the cabin. Niner One Echo, runway three five right, cleared to land. Do you need assistance? Negative, Niner One Echo. She lands, taxis in with the window open, shuts down, and sits on the step breathing. Marisol has the cowling off in ten minutes and the heat shroud off in twenty. A crack in the muffler about an inch long, black around the edges. Finally, Marisol says. Something actually broken. Jordan drives to her station and asks her partner to put the CO probe from the monitor on her finger. Seven percent. Her partner whistles. That's a smoker number. By noon the headache's gone, and Biscuit's grounded until Marisol finds a muffler.

Yep. That's the one. AIM 8-1-4 and the PHAK: with symptoms or a darkened detector while the heater's on, suspect CO, shut off the heater, open fresh air vents and windows, use oxygen if available, and land. Get checked if symptoms continue. Whatever leaked is a maintenance problem for the next pilot too.
Saturday, October 31. Ellie went as Biscuit.

It was a moving box out of Claire's garage. Arm holes. Two cardboard wings, duct tape. N4791E down the side in black Sharpie, the 4 a little backward, plus a maroon stripe in marker. The propeller was a paper plate on a brass fastener, and it spun if you blew on it. On the front, where the panel would be, she'd written HI DAD in purple. She walked the whole cul de sac in Parker with a pillowcase and told every adult who opened a door that the tachometer read fifty high.

At the house afterward Claire got two bottles out of the fridge and held them up like evidence. Have a beer with me. I've earned one and so have you. On the fridge door, under a magnet from a pizza place, was a school picture of Ellie in a green sweater, third grade, with two curled corners of old yellow tape still stuck to it. The tape caught Jordan's eye. She couldn't have said why.
Her next solo was 7 in the morning. The clocks went back tonight. She'd already thought about that, twice.
A. Two beers, the second one finished by nine. That leaves her a full ten hours before she flies.
B. A big glass of wine instead, since wine is lighter and she isn't much of a drinker.
C. Three beers, slow, done by 11:20. With the time change that's still over eight hours.
D. "Not tonight. I'm flying at seven." Water now, and she'll take Claire up on it next week.

Claire puts one back. The other she pops on the edge of the counter, Danny's trick, the one she always said she hated. You get a free hour tonight with the clocks. I'm spending it on sleep. I see what 'I waited eight hours' looks like at two in the morning. Everybody treats it like a target. From inside the box, Ellie: Is that a rule or a you rule? A me rule. Ellie considers this, propeller turning slowly. Those are the good ones.

Exactly right. 91.17 sets 8 hours and 0.04 as the legal lines, and the AIM recommends 12 to 24 hours between bottle and throttle. Zero drinks before an early flight is the simplest way to meet every part of the rule and the recommendation.
Sunday, November 1, the first morning on Mountain Standard Time, and the club chat woke up before Jordan did.
A message from Russ Kim. booked biscuit friday the 13th, KAPA to steamboat, back sunday. muffler's done right marisol
A message from Marisol Tran. New muffler, new gasket, shroud's clean. Ran it yesterday. The CO card is new too. Look at it.

A message from Russ Kim. back over the divide sunday at 13,500, about 45 min up there. no O2, i live at 5,800 feet, i'm basically a sherpa. jordan want to ride along? you can't log it but there's a burrito place
Jordan read it at the tie down with the engine still ticking. Walt hadn't said anything yet, which meant he was typing.
A. Reply with 91.211: past 30 minutes between 12,500 and 14,000, the crew uses oxygen. Bring it.
B. Point out that oxygen only becomes required above 14,000, so 13,500 is legal without it.
C. Tell him to stay at 12,500 or lower the whole way, so he never needs oxygen at all.
D. Say yes to the burrito. He's lived at altitude for years and he'll feel it if anything's off.

She types it with the section number, because she's her. 91.211(a)(1). Over 12,500 up to 14,000, crew has to use O2 for the part over 30 min. 45 min up there is 15 on oxygen. Also hypoxia's first symptom is feeling great. Sherpas carry oxygen. Walt: Thank you, Jordan. Marisol: Portable oxygen is in the cabinet, full, cannulas and the finger oximeter in the drawer. I'll show you Thursday, Russ. A long pause. Russ: cool. cool cool cool. Then: fine. i'll wear the nose hose. still a sherpa. jordan? She's working that Friday, the shift she traded for. She tells him to bring her a burrito.

That's it. 91.211(a)(1) requires the required minimum flight crew to use supplemental oxygen for any time beyond 30 minutes at cabin altitudes above 12,500 up to and including 14,000. The PHAK says everyone is susceptible regardless of acclimatization, and euphoria can be the first symptom.
Decision five. Sleep, meds, sick, anything.
Wednesday, November 4. She'd slept from eleven to three, which was four hours, and then she'd been on the kitchen floor with her back against the dishwasher, listening to the voicemail.

It was forty one seconds long, from the Thursday before. She'd never deleted it and she'd never played it, both on purpose, until three this morning. Hey. It's me. Ellie's got a game Saturday at nine, the fields by the rec center. Come if you're off. She's playing defense now, she's terrifying. Okay. Love you. Bye. She hadn't been off. She'd been on a twenty four, and at 9:40 that Saturday her phone had buzzed in the rig with Claire's name on it. She played it twice. Then she got up and made coffee because it was 3:20 and there wasn't any point.

6:50 AM at the tie down. Minus one, dead calm, frost on the wing that she'd toweled off and checked by hand already. Abby came around the tail with her coffee and the hood bag over one shoulder and asked the thing she always asked, same words every time. Sleep, meds, sick, anything?
A. "A little short on sleep, nothing else." It's true, and the birthday isn't Abby's business.
B. "Four hours, and tomorrow's his birthday. I want to fly. You should know that first."
C. "Ask me after. I'll know better once I'm in the airplane and the engine's running."
D. "Fine. Slept fine." Flying will take her mind off it, and she isn't going to explain the rest.

Abby sets her coffee down on the wing, carefully. She doesn't say she's sorry. Thank God. She just presses her lips together, the face she makes adding up hours on the back of a fuel receipt. Thank you. Okay, here's the deal. Dual, which it was anyway. Some hood work, nothing fancy, no pattern work alone. The minute it isn't there, you say so out loud and we go home. That still counts as a good lesson. Deal? Deal. Abby picks the coffee back up. Out loud. I'll hold you to that part.

Yep. That's the one. Fatigue and Emotion are both on IMSAFE, and the AIM says a pilot shouldn't fly after an emotionally upsetting event until recovered. Telling the instructor transfers part of the risk decision to someone who can see it from outside, the T in TEAM, and lets her set a clear way out.

7:50 AM, 7,500 feet over the stubble fields east of Bennett, about two thousand above the ground, the shelf at 8,000 overhead, and the sun low and white in the windshield. Abby had her under the hood, the foggles that cut off everything but the panel, for twenty minutes of straight and level and shallow turns, and Jordan had been fine. Better than fine. The attitude indicator was the only thing in the world, and it was very calm.
Okay. Demo. I have the airplane. You have the airplane. Eyes closed. Chin on your chest. Tell me what you feel.

She closed her eyes. Dark. Engine noise in her teeth. Level, it felt like, for a long while, then maybe a climb, then nothing she could name. For no reason her head went to a soccer field she'd never actually stood on, and then to the dishwasher at three in the morning. Head up. Eyes open. Recover. Your airplane.

The attitude indicator showed the little airplane banked thirty degrees right, nose well below the horizon. Airspeed 115 and climbing. Altimeter 7,320 and unwinding. Every nerve in her body said wings level and a gentle descent.
A. Lift the foggles and find the horizon outside, then fix the attitude by looking out the windshield.
B. Level the wings, then raise the nose smoothly, leaving the throttle right where it is.
C. Throttle back, level the wings on the attitude indicator, then ease the nose up to level.
D. Pull back firmly to stop the descent, since her body says the wings are already level.

Power back. Left aileron, some left rudder, eyes glued to the little airplane, and her whole body yells that she's rolling into a bank. She does it anyway. Wings level on the gauge. Back pressure, smooth. The airspeed bleeds off; the altimeter slows, stops at 7,240, turns around. Power in. 7,500. Power, wings, pitch. In that order. That's all it is. Inside her gloves her hands are wet. She never felt the bank. Not a degree of it.

Exactly right. The Instrument Flying Handbook's nose-low recovery: reduce power, correct the bank with coordinated aileron and rudder by reference to the instruments, then raise the nose with smooth back pressure. The AFH: believe the instruments regardless of what your senses say.

She flew the heading back toward the field and it wandered. Abby called traffic, a Cherokee at two o'clock low, and Jordan didn't hear it until the second time, and then couldn't find it, and then found it much closer than she liked. In a shallow climbing turn to give it room she let the nose come up, and when she looked, the altimeter said 7,780. Eighty feet over Abby's cap. Two hundred and twenty under the shelf. Abby tapped the glass with one fingernail and said nothing, which was worse.

Jordan fixed it. Seven seven hundred, seven six, level at 7,500. Her hands were fine. Her hands were always fine, that had never been the problem. Then the panel went blurry at the edges. She blinked and it came back, and then it went again, and it took her a good second to get that she was crying. A little. None of the rest of it, no noise, just the water, the way you sweat on a hot call.
Fifteen miles from the field. Forty minutes left on the lesson plan: hood work home, then three landings.
A. Push through like a bad call at work. Finish the plan, since stopping now means she failed.
B. Ask Abby to fly for ten minutes while she gets herself together, then do the landings.
C. Say nothing. Skip the hood, fly extra carefully, and do the three landings as planned.
D. "I'm not here today. Let's go home." She says it out loud, and they fly straight back.

Okay. Good. Abby doesn't take the controls. Your airplane, your radios. Straight back, no hood. You're doing the exact thing, by the way. This is the thing. Jordan wipes her face with the back of her glove and flies a heading of 270, and it holds. In the logbook that afternoon, in green, Abby writes LESSON TERMINATED BY STUDENT. GOOD CALL.

That's it. The AIM says a pilot shouldn't fly after an emotionally upsetting event until recovered, and the errors were stacking up. Saying it out loud uses the instructor as a resource and ends the risk at its source. 3P: she perceived it, processed it, and performed.

Twelve miles east, 7,500, she listened to the ATIS on the way in. Information Echo, one five one five Zulu. Wind three five zero at eight, visibility one zero, sky clear, temperature zero, dew point minus seven, altimeter three zero one eight. Landing and departing runway three five left. Runway one seven left, three five right, closed.

She'd written the NOTAM on her kneeboard at the kitchen table that morning at 5:40, after the coffee, before the tie down: 35R CLSD 1500Z TO 2300Z. And next to it, in her own hand, 9 AM. She'd subtracted six. It was November.

Centennial Tower, Cessna Four Seven Niner One Echo, twelve east, seven thousand five hundred, landing with Echo. Cessna Niner One Echo, Centennial Tower, make right base runway three five left, report two mile right base.

Right base, three five right, report two mile base, Niner One Echo. She heard herself say it. Nobody corrected her. The frequency was busy, a Citation and two students and somebody's long question about a taxi route. Abby, in the right seat, was looking out her window with great interest at nothing. Ahead, the long runway was coming up in the windshield the way it always did, the one she'd landed on two hundred times, with the shorter one beyond it, and something in the back of her head said left, and then closed, and then went quiet.
A. Ask tower to verify the runway before she turns final, and fly whatever they confirm.
B. Line up on 35L without a word. If 35R is closed she must have heard left, so it's fine.
C. Fly to 35R. She read it back, tower didn't correct her, and that's how a clearance works.
D. Ask Abby which runway tower said, since Abby heard the same call she did.

Centennial Tower, Niner One Echo, verify runway three five left? Niner One Echo, affirmative, runway three five left. Three five right is closed. Report two mile right base. Three five left, Niner One Echo. She looks down at her kneeboard. 9 AM. Fifteen hundred Zulu was eight o'clock. The runway she'd been aiming at had been closed for twenty minutes. Danny's line from the TAF entry came up word for word: In the winter it's seven, which I will also forget. She had. Abby, still looking out her window: Expectation bias, plus Zulu, plus four hours of sleep. You caught it. Fly the left one.

Yep. That's the one. A readback that ATC doesn't correct isn't a confirmation, especially on a busy frequency. When something nags, ask ATC to verify. The RMH describes expectation bias as hearing the usual clearance instead of the one given, and fatigue makes it worse.

Wednesday night she drove out to Parker with a quart of her mother's green chile on the passenger seat, because Lourdes had made too much for tomorrow and had decided Claire wasn't eating. Claire had just got in from the ER and was still in ceil blue, eating cereal over the counter.

Ellie came down in airplane pajamas. New ones, Jordan was almost sure. Mom said you had a bad flying day because you're sad about Daddy's birthday. She sat on the bottom step to think about it. Is sad a kind of tired? Jordan looked at Claire. Claire looked at the cereal. Yeah, El. It is. Okay. That's what I thought. And she went back up, and Jordan had to sit down on the step she'd left.

Later, on the back step, with tea neither of them drank, Claire said it. Four hundred and ten dollars a month, for eleven years. I did it on a calculator in March at three in the morning, which is when I do math now. Fifty four thousand one hundred and twenty dollars, before gas, before his part of the annuals. And Saturdays. Every Saturday morning I ever wanted, that airplane got first. She turned the mug in her hands. The one Saturday he skipped it was her game. He'd missed three in a row and he felt bad. So. She didn't finish, and Jordan didn't make her. I've been mad at a Cessna for seven months. It's exhausting. It didn't do anything.

And he got this thing. You only ever got the phone calls after. He called it a window. 'There's a window.' When Danny said window I started packing the car. The night before a trip he'd check the weather every ten minutes, and when it got worse he didn't cancel, he moved the time. Seven became six. Six became wheels up by five thirty. Once I found him in the garage at four in the morning loading the cooler in the dark so nobody would wake up and argue. He had a voice for it. Bright. Like a kid telling you about the lamp before you find it.

My sister's wedding, in Durango. The window over Wolf Creek was closing, so he wanted to go a day early, then he wanted to go that night. I said I'd drive. He flew alone, and he beat me there by six hours and met me in the parking lot with a coffee and that face. The short laugh. He was always fine. That's the thing about it. Every time he was fine, the next one got easier. You chart enough probably fine and you stop seeing it. She put the mug down on the step between them. So I'm going to ask you, because nobody ever asked him. Do you have it? The fever?
A. "This morning I did. I told myself I was fine. I'm writing my rules down before I need them."
B. "Maybe. I'll stop flying for a while, until his birthday and March are both behind me."
C. "No. I'm not him. I'm the careful one in this family, and today was one bad day."
D. "Everybody has a little. If you're scared of every cloud you'll never fly anywhere."

Claire nods slowly, looking at the dark yard. He wrote it all down after. Every time. Funny, so nobody would worry. She picks the mug back up. Write yours before. They sit there until the motion light over the garage clicks off. Neither of them gets up to wave at it. Somebody's dog two yards over barks about it for a while and then quits.

Exactly right. Personal minimums written ahead of time are the RMH's tool for exactly this, set when time and objectivity allow, never adjusted to make a flight happen. Admitting the hazard is the first step in the ADM process.

Thursday, November 5. Lunch at her mother's was pozole in the good bowls, and Lourdes set out six of them before she stopped, and stood there, and put one back in the cabinet without a word. Nobody said happy birthday. Her mother said the hominy was the wrong brand this year, twice, and that was how they said it.

At seven, the November safety meeting. Hangar Six, nine folding chairs, eight people. On the folding table by the coffee was a pink box of donuts, a dozen, and Walt stood next to it and didn't explain it. After a minute Marisol said, to nobody, He brought those every year. Closest meeting to his birthday. Said it was a tax. Russ took one and held it without eating it.

Before he started, Walt looked at Jordan over his glasses. Abby wrote 'terminated by student' in your book yesterday. First time I've seen that line in this club. Then he turned to the whiteboard, under Danny's capitals and Marisol's, and wrote five words: ANTI-AUTHORITY. IMPULSIVITY. INVULNERABILITY. MACHO. RESIGNATION.

He read from an index card. I read a report like this once. Doesn't matter where. There's a TFR for a wildfire twenty miles west of a pilot's home field. Pilot knows about it. Says, and it's in the report, 'TFRs are for news helicopters. Nobody tells me where I can fly my own airplane.' Flies straight through it to get a look. He capped the marker. Jordan. Which one, and the antidote. Word for word. The test wants the words.
A. Macho, since they're out to prove themselves near a fire. "Taking chances is foolish."
B. Anti-authority, because nobody tells them. "Follow the rules. They are usually right."
C. Invulnerability, as they assume nothing will happen. "It could happen to me."
D. Resignation, since they let the TFR decide nothing. "I'm not helpless. I can make a difference."

Walt writes it under ANTI-AUTHORITY in his small neat capitals. Good. You can question a rule. You file a question. You don't fly through it. He goes through the other four with cases of his own, and nobody eats a donut until he's done, and then everybody does. On the way out he stops beside her chair. Which one's yours? You don't have to say it here. She doesn't. In the car she writes it on the back of her hand with a pen from the glove box, the way he used to: MACHO. TAKING CHANCES IS FOOLISH.

That's it. "Nobody tells me" and treating a TFR as silly is anti-authority, "Don't tell me." The PHAK antidote is "Follow the rules. They are usually right." You can always question a rule you think is wrong, through the right channels.
Friday, November 6, two in the afternoon, the briefing room. Abby had texted the night before, after the meeting: Bring the worksheet. Tomorrow. I'll sit there while you do it.

The packet was where it had been for two weeks, in her flight bag, under the green notebook, with a coffee ring on the cover she didn't remember making. Abby slid a pencil across the table and a white index card, lined on one side. Worksheet's the thinking. Card's what goes in the airplane. Fill the worksheet from your logbook. Then the card.

Her logbook: 43.0 hours. Alone, 1.6, every tenth of it in the Centennial pattern. Windiest landing by herself, eight knots. With Abby, fourteen gusting twenty, and she'd rather not do that again soon. Shortest runway, 28, 4,800 feet. Highest density altitude, about 9,600, one August afternoon she'd worked out on a legal pad with Abby watching.
Abby didn't watch. She had her own logbook open and was adding again.
A. Write tighter weather and wind numbers than Abby's, and leave off the pilot part. IMSAFE covers it.
B. Build it from her logbook, inside Abby's limits, with her own lines for sleep, shifts, and dates.
C. Copy Abby's endorsement limits onto the card. Abby wrote them for her, so they're already personal.
D. Skip the card. Numbers make you rigid, and she'd rather decide fresh each day with IMSAFE and PAVE.

She works for forty minutes. The experience table first, every box, even the ones that say zero. Then the baseline. Then the adjustments, and she writes the handbook's rule at the bottom of the worksheet so she'll see it: don't change these to make a flight happen. Then the card, slowly, in block capitals. Abby reads it twice. No cross outs. One tap of her pencil on one line. This one. Most people don't write that one. Then, at the bottom: Two factors, go home. That's tighter than the book. I'll take it. She hands the card back. So where's it going? Airplane. Where in the airplane? Jordan doesn't answer that one yet.

Yep. That's the one. The RMH builds personal minimums from your own experience and comfort level, tighter than the regulations, with adjustments for pilot factors such as fatigue, stress, and emotion. Writing them before the pressure arrives is the whole point.

Saturday, November 7, 6:05 in the morning, the kitchen table, the card propped against the sugar bowl. Solo at 7:30, three laps, the slot she'd booked on Tuesday. Claire had texted last night that she'd bring Ellie by at nine to watch, on the way to the 10:30 game, the last one of the season. She wants to see you land. She made a sign.

KAPA, Saturday 5:53 AM. METAR KAPA 071253Z 34005KT 10SM SKC M02/M09 A3021 RMK AO2 SLP251 T10171089. TAF KAPA 071120Z 0712/0812 34006KT P6SM SKC. FM071600 32014G22KT P6SM FEW100. FM080000 33008KT P6SM SKC

She did the conversion out loud this time, slowly, like a dose. Sixteen hundred Zulu. Winter. Minus seven. Nine o'clock. Fourteen gusting twenty two, over every number on the card. The wind was coming the same hour Ellie was.
A. Cancel the solo. A wind change is coming, and showing Ellie the airplane on the ground is plenty.
B. Wait and fly at nine so Ellie can see. The TAF is only a forecast, and it's calm right now.
C. Take off at 8:30 so Ellie catches the last landing at nine, as the forecast wind arrives.
D. Go at 7:30 as booked, plan to be tied down by 8:30, and ask Claire to come at 8 if Ellie wants a landing.

She texts Claire at 6:10. Wind's due at 9. I'll be done by 8:30. Come at 8 for a landing, or come at 9 and we'll sit in her. Claire: We'll come at 8. She's already in her cleats. Runup on Alpha, ready for departure, monitor tower, and wheels up at 7:34. Two laps, smooth as glass. On the third downwind, at 8:04, the windsock by the tower lifts off its pole and swings, and the tower gives a Cirrus the wind, three two zero at nine, gusts one five. An hour early. One knot of gust over Abby's limit. She flies the last approach a little fast with a little more right wing down than she'd like, and puts it on, and calls it a full stop. At the fence, a nine year old holds up a poster board that says NICE LANDING in purple, which she'd made the night before, on faith.

Exactly right. The PHAK says to manage external pressure by managing passengers' expectations and leaving yourself an out. A forecast can be wrong in either direction, and here the wind came early. Flying in the calm window with a buffer, and moving the audience instead of the flight, kept her inside the card.

She'd read the next page of the notebook on Friday night, after the card, sitting on the floor of her apartment with her back against the couch instead of the dishwasher, which she counted as progress.

Danny's logbook, a page from February, eight years ago. Feb 3. KAPA, pattern, 0.7. El has had an ear infection since Tuesday and has screamed since Tuesday, and I have slept maybe 9 hours since then, total. Came out to clear my head. My head felt clear the whole time, I want that on the record. Landing 1: fine. Landing 2: flared at like twenty feet and she dropped like a piano. Landing 3: I remember the takeoff and I remember the flare and I do not remember the downwind. At all. Taxied in, sat in the car to warm up, woke up two hours later with Marisol knocking on the window holding a coffee. Claire had called four times. Lesson: tired doesn't feel like tired. It feels like fine. NEW RULE. Taped El's picture above the mag switch. If I can't look at her and say out loud that I slept, I go home. (Marisol says a picture isn't a rule. Marisol can mind her own business.)

She'd laughed at the last line, one bark, and then she'd stopped, because she knew where the picture was now. Third grade, a green sweater, two corners of yellow tape, under a pizza magnet on Claire's fridge.

Saturday, by 8:45, Biscuit was tied down with the chains tight and the wind coming hard out of the northwest, an hour ahead of the TAF. The NICE LANDING sign was propped against the left main tire. Ellie climbed into the right seat in her shin guards, which was allowed, because Biscuit wasn't going anywhere, and Claire stood at the open door with her arms folded against the cold.

He kept her picture there, Claire said, before Jordan could say anything, looking at the dark rectangle above the mag switch. Every September he put in the new school one. I took it down the week after. I couldn't stand it out here with nobody looking at it.
I know. He wrote it down.

Jordan got the white tape out of her jump bag, the inch-wide kind she used to hold down IV lines, and tore four strips with her teeth. She held the card over the rectangle for a second to see how it fit. It fit. Then she pressed down the corners, one at a time, right over the two yellowed ones he'd left.

Index card, taped above the mag switch. J. REYES. PERSONAL MINIMUMS. MINE, NOT THE FAA'S, NOT ABBY'S.. SOLO, KAPA PATTERN: CEILING 3,500 AGL. VIS 6 SM. WIND 10, GUSTS 5 OVER, CROSSWIND 5. IF IT'S CLOSE, IT'S NO.. 7 HOURS OF SLEEP OR I DON'T GO. NO SOLO THE MORNING AFTER A SHIFT.. NOTHING TO DRINK FOR 12 HOURS. SICK OR TAKING ANYTHING, I DON'T GO.. EMOTION IS WEATHER. MARCH AND NOV 5: DUAL OR NOTHING.. ONE FACTOR: ADD 500 FT, 1/2 MILE, TAKE 5 KNOTS OFF. TWO FACTORS: GO HOME.. I DON'T CHANGE THIS CARD IN THE PARKING LOT.
Ellie leaned over from the right seat to read it, mouthing the words. She knew where the picture used to be. You could tell from her face that she knew.

Emotion is weather, Ellie read, sounding it out the way she did spelling words at the kitchen table. That's a kind of weather? Mine, yeah. Ellie chewed the inside of her cheek. Daddy had my picture there. I know, El. Is a card better than a picture? There was no faking it with her. Jordan thought about it for real. No. This one's mine. The picture was his thing. Okay. Then, frowning at the card, like a teacher: You spelled everything right.
Under the card the HI DAD sticker had a corner up. Jordan pressed it flat with her thumb. Up it came again. Fine.

Claire stayed at the door with her arms folded for a while. Eventually she reached in past Jordan and pressed two fingers on the card, fast, the way you check a pulse on your way out of a room. He'd hate it. Not one joke on there. She took the hand back. It's good. A look at her watch. Ellie. Cleats. We're late, and I don't do late.
Ellie went over the seat back like a cat and paused on the step. Are you coming to my game?
It was the last one of the season. Ten thirty, the fields by the rec center. Jordan was off. She'd checked on Tuesday, without telling herself why.

Ellie sprinted for the car, braids blown flat sideways. Claire walked. Jordan stayed in the left seat another minute, hands on her knees, and read the card top to bottom once more, same as a run report before she signs it. Every line.
Her phone buzzed against her leg.
A text from Abby Strand. Practice area endorsement Tuesday after one dual. Then cross-country ground school. Buy a plotter. Not the fancy one. Bring the card, I want to see where you put it.
